item.title: How the US war has changed power equations in Iran
item.description: The fight is no longer about whether to bargain but the precise ways and means of improving Iran’s position before it commits to anything irreversible.
item.content:encoded:
When Washington unveiled its economic “D-Day” on August 19, the latest tightening of the financial siege and the blockade around Iran’s ports, it believed it was applying decisive leverage. But in Tehran the move was read as something else entirely – as confirmation that the US still prefers pressure to any settlement it might one day have to honour.

Across a political system that agrees on almost nothing, the interpretation was remarkably uniform. The economic stabilisers around the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, saw the US as reneging on a deal, while Ahmad Vahidi’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) commanders saw their own warnings about American perfidy vindicated.

So whatever faith remained in Iran about US willingness to close a deal has thinned further. That erosion of trust now shapes what Tehran will and will not accept.

It is important to realise that Iran is making existential decisions about the survival strategy of the Islamic Republic itself. The old vocabulary of reformist against principlist – or moderate against hardliner – no longer reflects the real struggle inside the system.

item.title: Fiction: A low-caste woman in Tamil Nadu’s Tranquebar is introduced to Christianity in 18th century
item.description: An excerpt from ‘The Grammar of Silence: Five Centuries. Three Women. Towards Liberation’, by R Seshasayee.
item.content:encoded:
Pecchi could not have guessed that the parangi who was leading her to this strange place was Schwartz – a man whose footsteps would later leave wide imprints on the soil of Thanjavur, whose name would one day be whispered as the shepherd of a new faith. For nearly 40 years, since Bartholomaeus Ziegenbalg had planted the first fragile seed of the Lutheran Mission in Tranquebar, Christianity had tried to push its tender roots into the hard earth of the south. The missionaries came from Denmark and Halle, carrying their strange books and stranger hopes – hoping to “rescue the heathen from darkness, to nurse their souls into salvation.”

But the land was old, its gods older still. The missionaries soon discovered that the people here clung fiercely to their pantheon, like children clutching the many fingers of one mother.

It was only with Schwartz’s arrival that the mission felt a new wind fill its sails.

Pecchi walked behind Schwartz towards the great doorway of the New Jerusalem Church, and a faint shiver passed through her. It was not entirely fear, nor entirely wonder, but something born of the two – like standing close to the sea at dusk, unsure whether to step back...

item.title: 7.8% GDP growth claim shaky, Centre must provide explanation, says Congress
item.description: The party asked why the numbers for the previous year’s April-June quarter were revised four times from around Rs 86 lakh crore to around Rs 80 lakh crore.
item.content:encoded:
The Congress on Thursday claimed that there was “growing evidence of irregularities” in the gross domestic product growth numbers released earlier this week, and said that the Narendra Modi-led government must explain the figures.

Congress leader Jairam Ramesh said that if the methodology behind the numbers was examined, “the whole thing starts looking rather shaky”.

According to figures released by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, the Indian economy grew by 7.8% in the April-June quarter. The Centre said that the manufacturing sector grew 9.2% during the first quarter of the financial year 2026-’27. This was up from 8.3% in the same period last year. The services sector grew 10%, compared with 8% a year ago, it added.

Ramesh noted on Thursday that the numbers for the previous year’s April-June quarter were revised four times from around Rs 86 lakh crore to around Rs 80 lakh crore.

“If you keep shrinking the base you’re comparing against, this year’s number will automatically look much bigger than it really is, even if nothing has actually changed on the ground,” the Congress said in a statement on social media. “That is simple arithmetic, not economic growth.”

item.title: Why Bangladesh should not join the Mecca Pact just to appease Pakistan or send a signal to India
item.description: The three members have pursued their own national interests, often at each other’s expense. Dhaka has no reason to behave differently.
item.content:encoded:
When Bangladesh’s Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman told parliament last week that Dhaka would view an invitation to join the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement positively, he framed the country's possible participation as “a measure for the self-defense of the global Muslim community”.

“It is an internal matter of the Muslim family,” Rahman explained.

In India, where the prospect of Bangladesh joining a defence pact founded by Pakistan has drawn considerable attention, that framing has understandably fed suspicion.

For readers on each side of the border, it would be worth trying to understand why the pact's existing members would want Bangladesh in the first place and what Dhaka stands to gain – or lose – by joining in.

The Mecca Pact, signed by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan on August 7, remains a loosely defined arrangement.

Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar has called it “purely defensive”, while Türkiye’s Hakan Fidan has likened its core clause to NATO's Article 5, which commits members to mutual defence.

Mechanisms for coordinating senior officials and armed forces are still being developed, and the pact lacks anything resembling NATO's integrated command structure.

item.title: Gloria Steinem, writer and feminist activist, dies at 92
item.description: One of the most prominent voices for reproductive rights, she spent two years in India in the 1950s and said the experience had a ‘huge influence on her’.
item.content:encoded:
Gloria Steinem, American writer and one of the most prominent activists for the reproductive and civil rights of women in the United States, died on Wednesday. She was 92.

She died at her home in New York, her foundation said on social media. “Gloria’s near-century on earth were years well-lived, and she continued working for equality until the very end,” it added.

Steinem started as a journalist in the 1960s, writing a feature on contraception that detailed how women were forced to choose between motherhood and careers. She followed this with an expose on sexism faced by cocktail waitresses at nightclubs owned and operated by Playboy Enterprises.

In 1971, she founded the Ms. magazine, a feminist publication that focused on problems faced by women.

She had moved from writing to public speaking after 1969, when she attended a meeting where women spoke up about the experience of having abortions, reported AFP.

Steinen had founded the National Women’s Political Caucus in 1971 with former US Representatives Bella Abzug and ​Shirley Chisholm and writer Betty Friedan.

item.title: Gloria Steinem (1934–2026): What we learnt from her 2015 memoir, ‘My Life on the Road’
item.description: One of the globally acknowledged leaders of second-wave feminism, Gloria Steinem died in her New York City home on September 2, 2026 at the age of 92.
item.content:encoded:
This article was originally published on The Conversation in 2018.

Gloria Steinem’s first book in more than a decade hit bookstores a couple of weeks ago. My Life on the Road proffers autobiographical snippets from what the famed feminist activist, journalist and author claims is the “most important, longest-running, yet least visible part of my life” – her nomadic existence on the road.

Steinem maintains that her intentions in relaying these experiences are manifold. Clearly, she wants to acquaint the public with this lesser-known facet of her itinerant life, but she also declares that she wants to “encourage you to spend some time on the road, too”; for us all “to share stories”; and “to open up the road – literally” given that “so far its been overwhelmingly masculine turf”.

But this book is also about setting the record straight. Steinem – who played a pivotal role in popularising second-wave feminism in 1970s America – is now a stately 81. This non-linear autobiography, then, is also an attempt to shore up her legacy in the so-called post-feminist age.

item.title: Bar councils have no power to punish law students, rules Supreme Court
item.description: The directions issued by the BCI chairperson to defer the enrolment of NALSAR’s graduating batch as advocates were unlawful, the court held.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Thursday held that the Bar Council of India and state bar councils do not have the statutory power to take disciplinary or punitive action against law students, Live Law reported.

The bar councils get disciplinary powers over law students only after they enrol as advocates, the court said.

It also held that the directions issued by Bar Council of India chairperson Manan Kumar Mishra on August 13 with respect to the graduating batch of students at the National Academy of Legal Studies and Research were unlawful, Live Law reported.

Mishra had directed state bar councils to defer the enrolment of the graduating batch as advocates after the students campaigned against inviting Chief Justice Surya Kant to their convocation over his remarks on police action against youth protesters. The Bar Council of India’s order had also sought an inquiry against the students and faculty members. The council, however, withdrew the directive hours later.

A day after the directive was issued, the Supreme Court had passed an interim order protecting NALSAR students and faculty members from punitive action by the Bar Council of India or any state bar council. Kant had described the bar council’s order as “absolutely uncalled for”.

At an event in New Delhi, Goyal claimed that India had secured a good deal in “every sensitive sector”, such as agriculture, fisheries and micro, small and medium enterprises.

He added that the country’s goods exports had continued to grow in August and urged industry associations to set ambitious export targets.

Goyal also pointed to India’s 7.8% gross domestic product growth in the April-June quarter, saying it was “no mean achievement” against the backdrop of global uncertainty. He urged stakeholders not to be swayed by “naysayers”.

The Congress had questioned the GDP numbers on Tuesday, describing them as “statistical gymnastics” being used to hide “India’s bleak economic reality”.

item.title: SC declines to hear plea challenging curbs on entry to government schools amid CJP campaign
item.description: The petition stated that the BJP governments in Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh were interfering with documentation being conducted in public interest.
item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court on Thursday refused to entertain a public interest litigation challenging orders by the Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan governments restricting the entry into public schools of outsiders, journalists, YouTubers and civil society representatives, Live Law reported.

The Bharatiya Janata Party government in both states had also mandated that permission must be taken for photography, videography, interviews, audio recording and livestreaming inside schools.

The orders had come against the backdrop of a nationwide drive of the Cockroach Janta Party political campaign to improve the condition of government schools. The campaign has been sharing videos of schools on social media recorded by its volunteers in several states.

The Rajasthan government had issued the order on August 16. In Uttar Pradesh, the basic education officer in Ayodhya issued a similar order on August 19.

The authorities in other districts of Uttar Pradesh, including Azamgarh, Ballia, Basti, Balrampur, Shamli and Agra, followed suit, Live Law quoted the petition as stating.

The petitioner argued that the restrictions violate the fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 14, 19 and 21 of the Constitution. The three articles protect the rights to equality, freedom and life and personal liberty.

item.title: A new book shows that in 1881, the Mysore Representative Assembly was already pursuing self-rule
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Longing for an Elsewhere: Mysore and the Making of India’s Developmental State’, by Chandan Gowda.
item.content:encoded:
Mysore was the first Indian state to have a representative assembly, a purely deliberative forum without powers of legislation whose members included landlords, merchants, and intellectuals nominated by the state. When the Mysore Representative Assembly (MRA) was founded in 1881, the editorial of a major newspaper published in British India noted:

“A new experiment is being tried in the Mysore state whose progress would be extremely interesting to watch because it has been frequently asserted that Eastern nations are not fitted for such councils or such a Government as that of England or the United States. For many centuries before our time, Hindoos have been despotically governed; so very few of them have actually taken part in the government of their country that they know not what real political freedom and true representative government mean.”

Colonial rule had revived older European views of oriental societies as historically subject to arbitrary despotic rule and therefore incapable of self-governance. The founding of the MRA was therefore an endeavour that could potentially prove the Indians’ capacity for self-government, although colonial discourses asserted otherwise. item.title: Census: Centre must justify collecting personal data, say ex-bureaucrats
item.description: ‘Much of this information appears to have little relevance for generating population statistics or informing public policy,’ they said.
item.content:encoded:
The Census 2027 questionnaire seeking details about the respondents’ parents, spouses and number of bank accounts requires justification from the Union government, said a group of former bureaucrats on Wednesday.

Such information should not be gathered “merely because it can be collected”, the Constitutional Conduct Group pointed out.

The questionnaire for the 2027 enumeration exercise includes 12 questions that were not asked in the previous census. These include questions seeking parents’ names, spouses’ names, permanent residential addresses, their nationality, the place where they got their Covid-19 vaccine, number of bank accounts, mobile phone, and details of Aadhaar, voter ID, passport and driving licence.

“Much of this information appears to have little relevance for generating population statistics or informing public policy,” said the group of retired bureaucrats in an open letter.

They also pointed out that some of the newly introduced questions, particularly those seeking details about the respondents’ religion and the place of birth of both parents, “could facilitate preparation or updating of the National Population Register, which in turn is associated with the proposed National Register of Citizens”.

item.title: ‘Gandhari’ review: Film about child sex trafficking is all a blur
item.description: Devashish Makhija’s thriller, written by Kanika Dhillon, is out on Netflix.
item.content:encoded:
It’s a particularly busy day in Joypurra town in Bengal. Bani (Taapsee Pannu) and her husband Gokul (Ishwak Singh) lose their daughter Mishty to sex traffickers. Bani suffers temporary vision loss while chasing the abductors. On this very day, police officer Kabir (Jatin Sarna) arrives in Joypurra, intent on dismantling the Blackhole trafficking gang.

Enraged by the local police’s apathy and undeterred by her condition, Bani decides to rescue Mishty all by herself. Her mother Jhunu (Mita Vashisht) happens to be around, concealing her ninja skills by selling jhalmuri. Blackhole’s leader Dada (Prashant Narayanan) keeps talking about a Plan Zero, which involves holding scores of abducted girls within Joypurra and waiting for the opportune moment to smuggle them out.

Kabir’s big idea to combat Dada’s ploy is to cordon off Joypurra. item.title: A decade since landmark law, disability rights and justice are stuck in a loop
item.description: The vision of the 2016 act to empower people with disabilities is unfulfilled while the key body through which rights were to be upheld has no real authority.
item.content:encoded:
A decade after the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act was passed, its vision of empowering people with disabilities and removing barriers to accessing justice is unfulfilled.

This failure is most evident in the functioning of the Office of the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities and its state counterparts, even though they were strengthened as part of the 2016 law to ensure substantive rights and meaningful access to justice for disabled persons.

The 2016 act envisaged a government-wide effort, requiring ministries, departments and public institutions to review and align their laws, policies, procedures and practices with its mandate.

In the absence of these reforms, persons with disabilities have been forced to assert their rights one legal case at a time. Contradictions in employment, education, accessibility, and public services quickly surfaced, with many disputes reaching the courts and generating a growing body of disability jurisprudence.

However, litigation was meant to be the exception, not the primary mechanism for securing rights guaranteed by law.

item.title: How a ‘super El Niño’ could make India’s monsoon drier – yet more dangerous
item.description: It could create an apparently contradictory situation: less rain over the season as a whole, but heavier rain when it does rain.
item.content:encoded:
India is currently in the middle of its summer monsoon, but this year’s rainfall presents an interesting paradox. Much of the country has received less rain than usual so far, yet has still been hit by severe floods and landslides. In Kerala, for example, devastating floods occurred despite the overall monsoon rainfall remaining well below average.

A weaker monsoon does not necessarily mean an absence of extreme rainfall. Rainfall can be highly uneven, with long dry spells broken by intense cloudbursts that cause flooding and landslides. This year’s experience in Kerala illustrates the apparent contradiction: a season that is dry overall can still produce devastating rainfall.

Amid this highly uneven monsoon, attention is also turning to something happening thousands of kilometres away in the tropical Pacific Ocean: El Niño.

It is well established that El Niño years, when certain parts of the Pacific are warmer than usual, are often associated with weaker Indian monsoon rainfall. Meanwhile La Niña – the opposite state to El Niño – tends to favour wetter conditions. This year, El Niño conditions have developed rapidly in the Pacific, with forecasts suggesting it could become exceptionally strong.

About a century ago, long before environmental degradation became the crisis of our times, Nobel Laureate Rabindranath Tagore had sounded early warning bells about the destruction of forests.

Though Tagore was born in the city of Kolkata, he had a deep and abiding contact with nature from childhood, and it shaped his many-sided genius in diverse ways. As an adolescent, he accompanied his father Debendranath to the foothills of the Himalayas, an experience he wrote about in his autobiographical notes.

Later, he was a frequent visitor to a zamindari estate in Shilaidaha, now in Bangladesh, where many of his short stories and songs were written while on a boat on the mighty river Padma. He had experienced the vast expanse of nature – in the sky, in the mountains, in the rivers and the flat, verdant lands of the Bengal delta.

item.title: ‘Maxxing’ is just self-care and improvement repackaged for social media
item.description: Constantly focusing on how to maximise ourselves may inadvertently cause us to become more focused on what is wrong with us.
item.content:encoded:
If you want to improve yourself, your health or your lifestyle, you need to do it to the “maxx” – according to social media, at least.

If you want to better your appearance, you need to try “looksmaxxing”. If you want to fix your diet and look after your gut, you should be “fibremaxxing”. And if you want to improve your social skills and be more charming, you really ought to be “personality-maxxing”.

But all of this maxxing might not actually be a good way to motivate yourself into healthier habits. In fact, it may have the opposite effect – and may even cause stress.

The language of “maxxing” has roots in the gaming concept of “min-maxing”, in which players strategically maximise desirable attributes while minimising less useful ones to create the most effective in-game character. The concept then made it’s way to the mainstream, most notably through “looksmaxxing”: making focused, and sometimes extreme, efforts to maximise physical attractiveness.

The suffix has since been adapted in multiple health and wellbeing spaces. If there is an aspect of life that could be improved, it can probably be maxxed.

item.title: How a male Marathi theatre star defined the role of the perfect Hindu wife in the 20th century
item.description: Bal Gandharva’s star persona became a site where respectable Hindu femininity was produced and commodified.
item.content:encoded:
For much of the 20th century, the most admired wife in Marathi-speaking India was not a woman at all.

Bal Gandharva (1888–1967), a celebrated impersonator of Marathi sangeet natak (musical theatre), played devoted heroines with such conviction that film actresses well into the 1970s were trained to reproduce his mannerisms.

How did a man come to define middle-class femininity with such authority?

My recently published research traces Gandharva’s enactment of womanhood from the stage to the marketplace.

It reveals how his star persona became a site where respectable Hindu femininity was produced and commodified – a project that the theatre industry, emerging consumer culture and Hindu nationalist politics each exploited for their own ends.

Staging respectability

India’s pervasive caste system divides Hindus into distinct groups based on which caste they are born into, with certain castes regarded as “higher” than others.

Some of these “lower” castes are made up of hereditary performers: families with a lineage of performing arts. Historically, women from these communities were allowed – and sometimes expected – to perform and entertain.

But Marathi sangeet natak, which emerged in the mid-19th century, was a predominantly upper-caste and middle-class practice.

When the Covid pandemic hit around March 2020, death itself lost its meaning because everyone was dying or was on the waiting list to hell. The wail of the ambulance, too, had lost its meaning because that sound had become the only noise in that deadly silence that had descended on the world. In Delhi, there was no space to bury the mounting dead. There was no farewell unless you treated the honking of the ambulance as a dirge or the drumbeats that herald Yama, the god of death. Bodies were being dumped all over. For a news photographer, it could be heaven or hell. How do you capture the inevitability of people dying in front of you? A 2026 review of the research examined the evidence on pulses and their effects on the gut and metabolism. Pulses are the dried edible seeds of legume plants, including lentils, chickpeas, dried beans and dried peas. Legumes are the wider plant family and also include foods such as soya and fresh peas.

The researchers brought together evidence from human studies with laboratory and animal research. So what does the science suggest pulses actually do once we eat them?

Pulses provide plant protein and fibre, along with carbohydrates that are not always completely broken down before they reach the large intestine.

It’ll not be a revision of her 2017 translation. She also added that the new edition will be longer and will “better reflect the differing social worlds of Homer’s poem.”

Wilson’s 2017 translation has sold more than a million copies. Peter Simon, her editor at WW Norton, told The New York Times that the book saw an uptick in sales after Christopher Nolan announced his movie. Nolan had cited her translation and its opening sentence, “Tell me about a complicated man,” as inspiration for his film. Wilson has, however, criticised Nolan for his adaptation of the epic and accused it of lacking “psychological, emotional, political and ethical depth.” She also said that the movie’s narrative structure was “gimmicky”, and the writing “abysmal.”

The new translation will also be published by WW Norton. Wilson said that she’s already halfway through and is a few years from completion.

item.title: For children: Why the Siberian crane that used to spend every winter in Bharatpur stopped visiting
item.description: An excerpt from ‘Gentle Sharks, Glowing Worms and Other Wonderfully Wild Creatures’, by Tara Gandhi.
item.content:encoded:
Bharatpur! The name always makes birdwatchers like me most excited since this town in Rajasthan is famous for the Keoladeo Ghana National Park, where thousands of waterbirds congregate. Migratory birds from far-off Arctic countries spend the winter months, escaping frozen landscapes to enjoy the warmer water of the Park’s wetland. Here they feast on abundant fishes, insects and water plants. It is certainly a birder’s paradise to be able to see so many species of ducks, geese and teals swimming in the deeper water, the waders along the shore, the raptors in the sky above, and arboreal birds on the bushes and trees surrounding the waterbody. Unlike other national parks and sanctuaries where the only way to see wildlife is on a jeep safari, here there are cycle rickshaws and bicycles for tourists to go around and one can even walk along the bunds of the waterbody. The rickshaw drivers are all trained guides who know the names of the hundreds of bird species – including their scientific names! item.title: Meghalaya: Four suspected members of armed group killed in gunfight with police
item.description: They were planning to abduct officials of the National Highways and Infrastructure Development Corporation Limited for ransom, alleged the police.
item.content:encoded:
Four suspected members of an armed group were killed in a gunfight with the Meghalaya Police in the East Garo Hills district on Sunday.

Two pistols, along with live and used rounds of ammunition, were recovered from them, said the East Garo Hills Police.

It alleged that the men were going towards Songsak town to abduct officials of the National Highways and Infrastructure Development Corporation Limited for ransom.

A team comprising personnel from the anti-terror squad, the East Garo Hills District Police and Songsak Police Station was deployed to intercept them.

At a checkpoint, when the vehicle carrying the four men was signalled to stop, they opened fire on the team, alleged the police. This prompted the security personnel to retaliate, it added.

The police said that the four men were taken to hospital, where they were declared brought dead.

They were identified as Allason Marak, a resident of Mendima in North Garo Hills, and Sustom Rabha, Kalam Ali and Bobidul Islam, all residents of Goalpara in Assam.

Marak was allegedly involved in a firing incident in Damra, in which a businessperson was killed, the police said. Rabha and Ali were allegedly accused in robbery, abduction and extortion cases.

item.title: Bangladesh says it is holding ‘positive dialogue’ on joining Makkah defence pact
item.description: Dhaka said that it sees no risk in entering into the agreement that was signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye on August 6.
item.content:encoded:
Bangladesh State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir on Sunday said that “positive dialogue” was underway regarding Dhaka joining the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, reported Prothom Alo.

The agreement was signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye on August 6 to strengthen “collective deterrence”. It states that an armed attack against any one of the three countries would be considered an attack against all.

The agreement had come against the backdrop of heightened tensions in West Asia amid the war involving Iran, Israel and the United States.

On August 11, India said that it was examining the implications of the agreement from the perspective of “national security as well as considerations of regional, peace and stability”.

Kobir said on Sunday that Bangladesh sees no risk in joining the pact, reported The Daily Star.

The pact brings together three Sunni Muslim-majority countries. Saudi Arabia is one of the world’s largest oil exporters and home to Islam’s holiest sites. Pakistan is the only nuclear-armed Muslim-majority country, while Türkiye has the North Atlantic Treaty Organization’s second-largest military.

In view of this, Kobir said that Dhaka views the pact positively “within the broader context of addressing challenges facing the Islamic world”, reported Prothom Alo.

item.title: How a Victorian philosopher found common ground between Hindu philosophy and socialism
item.description: In India, English philosopher Edward Carpenter found ideas of equality and social justice that echoed the socialist convictions he had developed in Britain.
item.content:encoded:
When Edward Carpenter arrived in Madras in 1891, he quickly discovered that being an Englishman in India came with a price. There were servants to employ, hotels to stay in and a standard of life to maintain.

Carpenter, a 46-year-old poet and philosopher, thought the whole arrangement was absurd. Using the term “John Bull”, a natural personification of England in political cartoons, he said his compatriots paid “through the nose” to maintain their privileges.

His own experience was hardly reassuring.

“As to the boatmen and drivers and guides and servants generally, they torment one like gadflies; not swindling one in a nice open riant way like the Italians of the same ilk, but with smothered dodges and obsequious craft,” Carpenter wrote in his 1892 book From Adam’s Peak to Elephanta, an account of his travels in Ceylon and India.

He complained about his last hotel in Madras, calling it “odious” with a “lying Indian manager” and “cringing servants”, including “an idiotic old man” who acted as his “boy” and tormented him by fiddling around with his slippers and holding a towel in readiness while he was washing his face.

item.title: Start the week with a film: ‘Scarface’ and the secret of its excess
item.description: Brian De Palma’s classic, led by Al Pacino, has many imitators and few rivals.
item.content:encoded:
After months of delays, Geetu Mohandas’s Toxic swaggered into cinemas last week, promising to re-examine its lead actor Yash’s hyper-macho image. While Toxic fired many blanks, the film’s over-the-top tone brought to mind another, much more successful attempt at using excess to depict excess: Brian De Palma’s Scarface (1983).

Based on both the 1930 novel of the same name as well as Howard Hawks’s adaptation with Paul Muni from 1932, De Palma’s Scarface has many imitators but few rivals. Endlessly quoted and referenced in both Hollywood and Bollywood, Scarface is the kind of movie that several directors try but few actually get.

Oliver Stone’s excellent screenplay sets the rise and fall of Tony Montana (Al Pacino) in Miami against American tensions with Cuba, the rising popularity of cocaine, 1980s bling and Giorgio Moroder’s synth-heavy score. Tony is a Cuban crook who gets entry into the United States by claiming to be a political refugee. Bursting with ruthlessness and chutzpah, Tony quickly rises up the ranks of Miami drug dealer Frank’s gang.

item.title: Why Tamil Nadu’s factories are death traps for migrant workers
item.description: The workers’ living quarters are often within or next to worksites. As the June tragedy in Tiruvallur showed, this exposes them to immense safety risks.
item.content:encoded:
At around 10.40 am on June 21, the female migrant workers’ quarters at a seafood processing plant in Tamil Nadu’s Tiruvallur district, was almost full. Many of the women were still sleeping because it was a Sunday, their day off.

The quarters were situated on the first floor of the plant, operated by St Peter and Paul’s Sea Food and Exports. The floor was also crammed with equipment, including refrigeration machinery, pipeline systems and an ice flakes generator machine.

Suddenly, the occupants began to feel breathless. Ammonia, a poisonous gas, was leaking up from faulty infrastructure in the plant below, and quietly filling up the room.

When news of the gas leak broke out, Kiran Kumar immediately rushed to the hospital where victims were being taken. Kumar is a social worker with Jesuits Migrant Services, which aids and advocates for the rights of migrant workers.

item.title: ‘Fake claims’: Great Nicobar lighthouse project study lists species found in Africa, Amazon
item.description: More than 90% of the species in the tables in the environmental impact assessment study for the Indira Point plan have never been reported from Great Nicobar.
item.content:encoded:
Species primarily found in Africa and the Amazon have been listed in a recent environment impact assessment study claiming that they live on Great Nicobar Island.

The report released in April was prepared by WAPCOS Limited, a Gurgaon-based public sector undertaking as part of a proposal to repair the lighthouse and construct tourist facilities at Indira Point, the southern-most point of the island – and of India.

Tables in the environment impact assessment report list tiger fish (Hydrocynus vittatus), a native of African freshwater rivers, and the flagtail (Semaprochilodus insignis), an Amazonian freshwater fish.

Also listed are sambar (Cervus unicolor) and barking deer (Muntiacus muntjak), two species of mammals found primarily on India’s mainland.

More than 90% of the species listed in the tables in the study have never been reported from Great Nicobar. In many cases the closest sites are thousands of kilometres away.

Ecologists and marine biologists who have spent decades studying Great Nicobar said the report was “shocking” and alleged that it was “completely fabricated”.

The study includes the Eurasian woodcock (Scolopax rusticola), a bird of temperate and subarctic Eurasia that is found in Sri Lanka and along India’s western coast only in the non-breeding season, and the Mayabandar rice frog (Microhyla chakrapanii), which has only ever been reported from the Andaman Islands but not the Nicobar.

item.title: Microfinance promised economic freedom but created more debt for the poor
item.description: It was aimed at low-income households in Asian countries, including India, typically excluded from traditional banking.
item.content:encoded:
Microfinance was once celebrated as Asia’s tool to lift people out of poverty. From Bangladesh to India, Cambodia and the Philippines, the promise was simple: provide small loans to low-income households, help them start businesses, increase income and escape poverty.

Pioneered in the 1970s, microfinance was designed to provide financial services to low income people typically excluded from traditional banking.

Small loans, usually between US$200 and US$500 (about Rs 19,000- Rs 47,000 at current exchange rates) were particularly targeted at empowering women to start businesses and support their families. According to the World Bank, more than 1.7 billion people do not have access to banking.

Yet decades of experience suggest that credit alone has not delivered the transformation to economic independence promised.

We need to ask a difficult question: what if we solved the wrong problem?

Based on flawed assumptions

One fundamental problem is the assumption that poor households in developing nations lack capital but have profitable investment opportunities.

In reality, many poor families operate very small businesses such as food stalls, small shops, farming, tailoring or petty trading. These activities are often labour intensive and face intense local competition.

item.title: ‘The Mistress of Phoolpur’: These short stories promise interesting ideas but fall short on delivery
item.description: A greater leap of faith by author Pratyaksha would have encouraged an empathetic understanding of desire and its consequences.
item.content:encoded:
A friend once described watching an Odissi dance troupe perform the same piece in multiple locations over the course of a few weeks as an experience that provided diminishing returns. The initial appreciation turned sour by the third viewing – he summed it up as a lot of yearning for a distant lover with the dancers dashing from one corner of the stage to the other. The only thing that briefly perked him up was the lead dancer spraining her foot and bravely limping through the the final performance. She kept up the yearning though, he said.

Odissi and two of its great contemporary practitioners, Surupa Sen and Bijoyini Satpathy, are the muses of “You Were My Death”, a story in Pratyaksha’s new collection of short fiction, The Mistress of Phoolpur. item.title: As Tibetan plateau turns into a cascading danger, China’s control complicates cooperation on safety
item.description: Strengthening cross-border data-sharing and early-warning systems would reduce the lethality of earthquakes, landslides and floods.
item.content:encoded:
Within the space of a few minutes on August 26, the border crossing between Nepal and China – Rasuwagadhi on the Nepali side and Gyirong on the Chinese – was destroyed by a flash flood caused by a collapsed glacier. Villages, bridges and roads on both sides of the border were washed away.

Hundreds are dead and many more missing, including tourists and pilgrims. The full toll will not be known for days as the worst-hit areas are hard to reach. In the case of Tibet, given the history of China’s draconian control over information, the true toll may never be known.

Already impoverished, Nepal faces grave challenges of rebuilding once the relief effort is over. This is the first real test for the government that took power in March after a successful gen Z revolution swept away the traditional parties.

Prime Minister Balen Shah’s government has tried to avoid becoming dependent on either large neighbour, China or India, or trapped in their rivalry. It has asserted some strategic autonomy by dealing with New Delhi, Beijing and Washington on an even footing.
